issues.legal_issue: The non-compoundability of an offence does not, by itself, prevent the High Court from quashing its prosecution under its inherent jurisdiction.
material_facts: The prosecution included an offence that could not be compounded under the statutory list of compoundable offences.
The accused sought quashing of the pending prosecution on the basis of a settlement between the parties.
issues.conclusion: The High Court may quash a prosecution for a non-compoundable offence where doing so is necessary to secure the ends of justice or prevent abuse of process; the statutory restriction on compounding does not control that inherent power.
issues.legal_principle: Section 320(9) of the Code of Criminal Procedure restricts compounding to offences listed as compoundable, but it does not limit the High Court’s separate inherent power under Section 482. Ram Lal v. State of J & K and Ishwar Singh v. State of Madhya Pradesh establish that a non-compoundable offence cannot be compounded, while State of Karnataka v. L. Muniswamy, Madhavrao Jiwajirao Scindia v. Sambhajirao Chandrojirao Angre, B.S. Joshi v. State of Haryana, Madan Mohan Abbot v. State of Punjab, Nikhil Merchant v. CBI, and Manoj Sharma v. State support quashing in an appropriate case to secure justice or prevent abuse. The power is discretionary, must be exercised sparingly and with care, and is not a licence for the High Court to assess evidence as an appellate court.

predicates.inherent_quashing_proceeding: A party asked the High Court to use its inherent jurisdiction to end a criminal prosecution.
predicates.offense_not_compoundable: The prosecution includes an offence that the law does not permit the parties or the trial court to compound.
predicates.quashing_needed_for_justice: The circumstances show that ending the prosecution is necessary to secure justice or prevent abuse of process.

issues.definition: When a party seeks inherent-jurisdiction quashing of a prosecution for an offence that cannot be compounded, the High Court may quash it if ending the case is necessary to secure justice.

issues.legal_issue: A prosecution for a non-compoundable offence may be quashed after settlement where the dispute is personal and continuing the trial would be futile and an abuse of process.
material_facts: The incident arose from a dispute about access to adjoining plots and was not a robbery for gain.
The parties settled the dispute, and the complainant stated that she no longer supported the allegations, describing the complaint as arising from misunderstanding and misconception.
The complainant’s husband and brother, who were the other alleged eyewitnesses, also no longer supported the prosecution version.
The Court concluded that there was no realistic prospect of conviction and that continuing the trial would be an empty and wasteful exercise.
issues.conclusion: The High Court should have exercised its inherent power to quash the prosecution; the Supreme Court allowed the appeal and quashed the proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, the High Court may quash a prosecution, including one involving a non-compoundable offence, when the facts show that continuation would be futile and an abuse of process or would not serve the ends of justice. The Court applied the principles in State of Karnataka v. L. Muniswamy, Madhavrao Jiwajirao Scindia v. Sambhajirao Chandrojirao Angre, B.S. Joshi v. State of Haryana, Madan Mohan Abbot v. State of Punjab, Nikhil Merchant v. CBI, and Manoj Sharma v. State, while emphasizing that the power is discretionary and must be exercised with care.

predicates.inherent_quashing_proceeding: A party asked the High Court to use its inherent jurisdiction to end a criminal prosecution.
predicates.noncompoundable_charge_in_case: The prosecution includes an offence that the parties cannot compound under the law.
predicates.dispute_arose_from_personal_or_civil_con: The alleged criminal incident arose from a personal or civil dispute rather than an independent crime for gain.
predicates.parties_settled_dispute: The parties resolved the dispute between them.
predicates.complainant_will_not_support_prosecution: The complainant stated or otherwise showed that she would not support the allegations at trial.
predicates.material_witnesses_will_not_support_pros: The other material witnesses were also no longer supporting the prosecution version.
predicates.trial_would_be_futile: The circumstances showed that a trial was unlikely to result in conviction and would serve no useful purpose.

issues.definition: A prosecution should be quashed when a personal or civil dispute has been settled, the complainant and material witnesses will not support the case, and a trial would be futile.

issues.legal_issue: An offence of assault or criminal force against a woman with intent to outrage her modesty is compoundable at the instance of the woman against whom it was committed.
material_facts: The appellants were charged with an offence under Section 354 of the Indian Penal Code.
The alleged victim settled the matter with the accused.
issues.conclusion: The alleged victim’s settlement permitted the charge under Section 354 to be compounded.
issues.legal_principle: Section 320(2) of the Code of Criminal Procedure makes an offence punishable under Section 354 of the Indian Penal Code compoundable at the instance of the woman against whom it was committed.

predicates.criminal_proceeding_includes_assault_on_: A criminal proceeding includes an allegation of assault or criminal force against a woman with intent to outrage her modesty.
predicates.affected_woman_agrees_to_compounding: The woman against whom the alleged offence was committed agrees to compound it.

issues.definition: An assault-on-a-woman offence of this kind may be compounded when the woman against whom it was allegedly committed agrees.
